title: Devanagari
hook: a line of letters on a wedding card: why learn to read what already works when it's chanted?
tomorrow: a line runs across the top of the letters. what's it holding up?

segments.voice: Yesterday, year 4, the ranges: a scribe whose pen must not stop, and a poet who asked him to understand every line first. Year five starts where a scribe would, with the letters.

A wedding card on the fridge. A sticker on a laptop. A line of text under a photo in the family group chat. Letters with a flat bar running along the top, each one hanging from it like laundry on a line. Some people read it at a glance. To others it's a row of beautiful shapes. That script is Devanagari, and year five opens with it. So, one question for today: if a sacred line already works when it's chanted, why learn the letters at all?
screen: `A LINE OF LETTERS ON THE FRIDGE.` → `LETTERS HANGING FROM A BAR.` → `WHY LEARN THE LETTERS AT ALL?`

segments.voice: Here's one answer the tradition gives, from the Bhagavad Gita. In chapter ten, Krishna names the places he can be found: among mountains, among rivers, among seasons. And among letters, he says, I am a. Not a temple, not a star. A letter. Some readers notice something about the script itself. In Devanagari, a consonant written alone is never silent: it carries a short a inside it. Ka, not k. Ga, not g. Unless a small mark takes it away, a is there in the letter, the way the Gita says the divine is there in the world. Then the word for a letter: akshara. It also means the imperishable, what doesn't wear away. The Gita uses it both ways. In chapter eight, the akshara is the highest, the imperishable. In chapter ten, aksharas are letters. So learning to read isn't only homework before the real thing. The letters can be a way in. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words. Muslim tradition holds that the first words revealed to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, were a command to read. In Pickthall's translation of the Qur'an: "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth." And a few lines on: "Who teacheth by the pen, Teacheth man that which he knew not." Two traditions, each putting something holy right beside learning your letters. And one honest difference. In the Qur'an's words, God is the one who teaches, and the pen is how. In the Gita's words, Krishna is found in the letter itself.
screen: `AMONG LETTERS, I AM A.` · `A SHORT A INSIDE EVERY LETTER.` · `AKSHARA: A LETTER, THE IMPERISHABLE.` · `READ: WHO TEACHETH BY THE PEN.` · then, large: `THE LETTERS CAN BE A WAY IN.`

segments.voice: Let a soft, open sound ride out on each breath: a, the way it sits inside ka and ga, mouth relaxed, no effort. Breathe in quietly, sound it on the way out, and let it fade into silence before the next breath. Krishna's letter, said for as long as the bell runs.
Devanagari: the script with the bar along the top, used for Sanskrit, and for Hindi and Marathi too. Its letters are aksharas. Year five's first word.
For the road: Devanagari, letters with a sound already inside them. Year five, day one.

howItsDone: Hindu children and adults learn Devanagari at home, at weekend classes and from teachers who chant verses with them; some begin a new subject or school year by writing their first letters before Saraswati or Ganesha.

notes: Recipe v3, wisdom shape. Question: why learn the letters if the chanted line already works? Answer: Gita 10.33 (among letters Krishna is a) and akshara as both letter and imperishable (Gita 8.3 and 10.33). Unity thread: Qur'an 96:1-5 (Pickthall 1930) on reading and the pen, with one honest difference (God teaches by the pen vs. Krishna found in the letter). No ranking.

The inherent short a in Devanagari consonants (and the virama that removes it) is a standard fact about the script, introduced with 'some readers notice' as a reading of 10.33, not as the Gita's own claim or any commentator's. Confirm.
